Every answer the Investment Analyst wrote in the four layers behind this memo, word for word
The Financial Analyst Memo: every financial table and model output behind this memo

QT Group: a well-founded 2027 earnings restoration at a low multiple, waiting for proof of organic growth

14 November 2026. Share price EUR 30.48 (11 November 2026); market value about EUR 0.77 billion; enterprise value about EUR 0.85 billion.

How to read the numbers. Money is in EUR. Two EPS bases are in use, and in 2027 they differ by about EUR 0.39 a share. The model basis is before the amortisation of acquired intangibles. The consensus basis is after that amortisation, which is how three of the four brokers report. Every EPS figure below names its basis. "Underlying" means before restructuring costs. EBITA is QT's own operating-profit measure, before the amortisation of acquired intangibles. Sources and bases are in the end notes.

0. Summary: key insights, implications and conclusions

QT Group sells the software tools that engineers use to build devices with screens and embedded software. Its products are the Qt user-interface framework (developer seats sold on subscription, plus a royalty on each device shipped), testing tools and, since October 2025, IAR's certified compilers. QT leads its niche by a wide margin, its customers almost never leave, and it raised prices through its worst year in a decade.

The answer to Richard's testThe share value is skewed to the positive today, but the probability of earnings upgrades is not. The upgrade skew can open with the first-quarter 2027 report in late April or May 2027, if organic growth excluding IAR reaches 6-7%.

The case in three years.

  • 2025 broke the growth story: organic growth fell to 2.6% against a cost base built for growth of 15-25%.
  • 2026 absorbed the repair: a restructuring, a deliberate revenue trough at IAR as it moved to subscriptions, and guidance reset to floors.
  • 2027 shows the result: model-basis EPS of EUR 2.31 against EUR 1.53 in 2026, and an EBITA margin of about 29% against about 21% reported for 2026 (about 25% underlying).

About four fifths of the 2027 earnings step rests on actions the business has already taken. Yet the shares trade on about 13 times consensus earnings two years ahead, the 7th percentile of their own history and a little below the sector median.

What I conclude.

  1. The 2027 earnings step is the predictable core of the case, and consensus already holds it. Three independent builds of 2027 EBITDA (the model's, consensus and management's "about 30%" operating-margin ambition) sit within 3% of each other, so this memo holds no numerical edge over the sell-side on the next two reports.
  2. The favourable gap lies in the multiple, and only evidence of demand will close it. Investors have paid for the removal of downside risk and nothing for cost-led upside. In six months consensus 2027 EPS rose 46% while the share price rose 30%, so the multiple fell; and the shares fell 16% after a 7% revenue beat in October. The first report that can show clean organic growth is for the first quarter of 2027, due in late April or May.
  3. The range of 2027 earnings is skewed down, but the share value is skewed up. The 2027 EPS range runs about 27% below the base case and 15% above it. The starting multiple is low enough that I see EUR 18-22 a share in a bear case, about EUR 36 by March 2028 with no re-rating, and EUR 47-58 at the 16 to 20 times that the evidence supports.
  4. The guideline fair multiple of 43 times, and the modelled return of +359% built on it, are not supported by the evidence. Without the re-rating, the same model returns +15% by March 2028; the remainder depends on a multiple that QT earned when it grew 20-50% a year.
  5. The upgrade skew Richard looks for is absent today and can open in spring 2027. Guidance is a floor that will be beaten but not raised, consensus sits on my base case, and the momentum of estimate revisions will fade by arithmetic. QT is a well-founded earnings restoration at a low multiple, waiting for its second act: proof of organic growth of 6-7% or better.

The five judgements that move the value most (sized in topic 9) are: organic growth excluding IAR in 2027; royalties; how much of the cost saving is reinvested; the effect of AI on the number of developer seats; and the dollar.

Ratings and scorecard

1. Tailwinds and headwinds in the operating environment

Evidence. Demand troughed in 2025, when QT's organic growth was the lowest since 2014. The recovery since 2025 is real but narrow: European developer licences, Chinese carmakers, defence and aerospace, and medical customers are growing, while the United States (about a third of revenue), Western carmakers and industrial automation are not. About half of QT's revenue comes from cyclical end-markets.

The two newest automotive data points pull in opposite directions. S&P Global has cut its 2027 light-vehicle production forecast to −0.2%, with China the weak region (reported by Jefferies on 12 November). Two days earlier, Infineon guided to mid-teens automotive growth as its customers restock.

The structural forces mostly favour QT, but they act slowly. The EU Cyber Resilience Act applies in full from December 2027, and Qt 6.12 is the first Qt release with a signed declaration of conformity, which gives open-source users a reason to buy a commercial licence. AI-generated code raises the volume of code that must be tested. Against that, AI also raises output per engineer, and almost all developer-licence revenue is charged per seat.

Competition is quiet where QT earns its money. Google's Flutter has stepped back from embedded work, and no commercial rival attacked during QT's weakest year; only the free libraries LVGL and Slint are gaining, at the cheap end of the market.

QT's currency exposure is large and open: 62% of revenue is in foreign currencies against 32% of costs, and none of the exposure is hedged.

Inference. External forces will add little to 2027 by themselves. The model's 2027 organic growth of 6.5% assumes no restart in Western automotive R&D, and nearly half of that growth is price. Over three years the external balance is better than neutral, because the cyclical drag has little further to fall while demand for compliance and testing builds.

So what. The case does not need an external tailwind. It needs Western industrial R&D spending to avoid a second leg down during the two December quarters that decide QT's 2026 and 2027 results.

Counter-case. A tariff-led, synchronised automotive and industrial recession, to which I give a probability of about 15% over 18 months, would cut royalties by a quarter to a third and freeze seat purchases, taking 25-40% off 2027 EBITA. The Cyber Resilience Act's pull may also be weaker than hoped, because about 90% of connected products fall in the class that allows manufacturers to self-assess their compliance.

Against the market. The market treats QT as an AI-exposed cyclical and pays the sector's depressed multiple for it. I agree that the environment alone earns no higher multiple. I differ on one point: the market's narrative reads royalties as a proxy for car production, and the evidence says otherwise. Medical is the largest vertical at about 20%, automotive is 10-15%, and the royalty line moves with prepaid blocks and single deals of EUR 1.5 million or more. Year-end deal timing therefore matters more to royalties than S&P's production forecast does.

What would change my view. Positively: two consecutive quarters of growth in US developer licences, or royalties up more than 10% for two quarters. Negatively: royalties down more than 5% for two quarters, or more peers reporting delayed enterprise deals, as TeamViewer did on 3 November.

Conclusion: The operating environment is a fading cyclical headwind and a slow structural tailwind: enough to support mid-single-digit organic growth, but not enough to drive the case.

Score: 55, set by the Rater. A fading cyclical drag (Western carmakers, industrial automation, US developer demand flat, S&P cutting 2027 light-vehicle output) against slow structural pulls (Cyber Resilience Act from December 2027, more AI-generated code to test, Flutter's retreat from embedded), net of LVGL/Slint at the cheap end and AI's threat to seat counts; the 80th-percentile consensus sales growth is mostly IAR consolidation and price, which are the company's own, so the external balance is only a mild positive supporting mid-single-digit organic growth, in line with the 57 group score.

2. Internally driven corporate change

Evidence. The cost reset is large, funded and mostly done; the tiles below give its size. The gross savings of about EUR 23 million a year combine the EUR 20 million programme with EUR 3 million from closing IAR's security unit.

IAR is moving its customers from perpetual licences to subscriptions faster than planned. The faster conversion cut IAR's 2026 revenue by EUR 5-10 million and sets up growth from 2027.

Management has rebased its stated ambition from growth of 20-30% a year to organic growth of about 10% with an operating margin of about 30%. Large acquisitions are paused and debt is being repaid. New products have shipped on time (the AI design tool Clate has been in beta since October), and the company now publishes annual recurring revenue (ARR) and royalties every quarter.

The problems sit one layer below the chief executive. The CFO, the head of sales, the head of IAR and two successive heads of the testing unit have changed within 18 months, and testing, the unit meant to grow fastest, has had no permanent head since October 2025. On 29 October the chief executive said he was not happy with US sales, a year into the effort to fix them. The 2025-2027 share plan pays out only if 2027 revenue exceeds EUR 333 million, so it is worthless as a retention tool. Management has also said that part of the savings will be reinvested, without giving an amount.

Inference. The reset is profit-first, led by an owner-backed chief executive who accepted visible damage to 2026 in exchange for a stronger 2027. Management's force is strong in the part of the income statement that it controls and weak where the valuation is decided: organic growth, the United States and the leadership of testing.

So what. The 2027 margin step is likely. Its size is the open question, and the size turns on about EUR 5 million of reinvestment, worth about 2 points of margin.

Counter-case. Cutting 18% of staff in the same year as an integration and a subscription conversion can damage the selling engine, and sector precedents divide on whether it does. Truecaller and Yubico restored their margins within two or three quarters of cutting because their revenue held; Cerence did not, because its royalties fell.

Against the market. The brokers know the self-help and model it in full. I differ from the share price in my confidence that the self-help will deliver. The 2027 forecast needs revenue per employee only about 5% above the 2024 level, after three years of price increases of about 5% a year, so it asks the business to do nothing it has not done before.

What would change my view. Underlying fourth-quarter costs well above EUR 46 million; a 2027 margin floor of 22% or less; further departures in sales or testing; or evidence that IAR's converted customers do not renew.

Conclusion: Internally driven change is strong, largely executed and enough to carry 2027; its cost is execution strain in the management layer below the top two decision-makers.

Score: 68, set by the Rater. A large, funded, largely executed reset (18% of staff gone, about EUR 23m of savings worth over 40% of 2025 EBITA, EUR 9.7m of charges ending, IAR's subscription conversion at 68% against a 40% plan, debt being repaid) drives most of a 51% EPS step in 2027 and is already visible in headcount and two beats; it is repair rather than growth, ambition was rebased down, and the churn of CFO, sales, IAR and testing heads with US sales still unfixed hold it below the 75s, a little above the 62 group score because the earnings effect is unusually large and sure.

3. Value chain, competitive advantage, financial profile and management

Evidence.

Industry and position. QT is the leading commercial vendor of cross-platform user-interface frameworks for embedded devices, several times the size of its next commercial rival. It has about 1.5 million developers and more than 3,500 customers, none of which exceeds 10% of revenue. QT sits at the most profitable point of its value chain: its suppliers have no leverage, and chipmakers pre-integrate its tools into their reference designs, which works as free distribution.

Advantage. Customers face three switching costs: rewriting the interface, retraining engineers and re-certifying safety-relevant software. Free alternatives lack the safety certifications that regulated products need. The 2025 downturn proved the advantage. Guidance was cut twice, the shares halved and the sales organisation was in disarray, yet no rival undercut QT, prices rose and churn stayed low; the downturn showed only in seat numbers, contract length and royalty volumes.

Financial profile. QT's economics are excellent (tiles below), with two blemishes. First, about 95% of a contract's value is recognised at signing, so reported revenue follows contract length and December signings as much as usage. Second, the return on capital employed fell from 43% to 15.5% after the EUR 205 million purchase of IAR, which earns about 7-8% before tax by 2028 before any cross-selling.

Management. The chief executive has run the business since 2016, holds about EUR 12 million of shares and has the backing of a chair whose group owns 21.6%. Governance is clean and communication is unusually candid. Against that, growth guidance was missed four years running (2022-2025), the management bench is thin, decisions rest on two people with no visible successor, and the company has never returned cash to shareholders.

Inference. QT is a high-quality franchise with a cyclical, lumpy income statement and a deal-minded capital allocator. Its competitive structure protects price and market share. The structure does not protect the number of seats, which AI may reduce, or QT's position in cheap devices, the segment from which future royalty growth must come.

So what. The foundations support the model's two steadiest assumptions: a realised price rise of about 4.5% a year and an EBITA margin that returns above 30%. Once growth is visible, the same foundations would support a multiple above the sector's.

Counter-case. AI coding agents could make it cheap to port an interface to another framework, eroding the rewrite cost in unregulated devices. Carmakers could back a royalty-free framework. Android Automotive could win safety certification and move from the infotainment screen to the instrument cluster.

Against the market. At about the sector-median multiple, the market prices QT's quality as average. I rate the franchise in the top quartile, and I accept a discount for the forecasting record and for capital allocation.

What would change my view. Rising churn at renewal, a pause in price increases (TeamViewer paused its own increases for small customers this year), or the loss of a flagship automotive platform.

Conclusion: QT's foundations are strong in structure, advantage and economics and only average in management depth and capital allocation: a better base than the current multiple credits.

Score: 72, set by the Rater. Qualitatively strong: the leading commercial embedded user-interface framework at the most profitable point of its chain, three switching costs and safety certification proven in 2025 when prices rose and churn stayed low, licence gross margins above 80%, near-zero capital spending and free cash flow above net income (return on invested capital at the 77th percentile, free cash flow margin at the 85th); held below 75 by low predictability (upfront recognition, December concentration, four missed growth guides), the EUR 205m IAR earning only 7-8% pre-tax, a thin bench and the open AI question on seats, coherent with the 60-76 groups.

4. Conservatism of guidance and the record of delivery

Evidence. Formal 2026 guidance consists of two floors: revenue growth of at least 10% at constant currency and an EBITA margin of at least 15%. IAR's consolidation alone supplies about 11 points of growth, so the revenue floor needs no organic growth at all. To meet the floors, QT needs fourth-quarter revenue of only about EUR 72 million and EBITA of about EUR 16-17 million, far below what the model and consensus expect (chart below). Management reiterated the floors three times while nine-month growth ran at about 21%. It has also told analysts not to model revenue from new pricing, to expect royalties flat or slightly lower, and to assume that part of the savings is reinvested.

Management's delivery record has two halves (table below). Promises about costs, integration and subscription conversion have been met or beaten. Growth guidance was missed in each of the last four years, cut twice in 2025 and never raised, while margin guidance was met in 2023 and 2024. Against consensus, revenue beat in three of the last four quarters, from a low bar.

Inference. Guidance is now conservative in form and carries no information about the upside. Management adopted floors to stop the downgrades, and the floors did stop them. I expect the same form for 2027 (about 70% likely), at something like growth of at least 5% and a margin of at least 25%, set below consensus by design and then left unchanged.

So what. Investors should not look to guidance for upgrades; the level of the 2027 margin floor, due on 18 February 2027, is the signal to read. A floor of 27% or more signals confidence, and a floor of about 25% matches my base case. A floor of 22% or less, or the disappearance of the informal "about 30%" margin ambition, would show that reinvestment is absorbing the savings and would take 3-5% off 2027 estimates.

Counter-case. A management that has learned to under-promise could now beat in every quarter, as it did in the second and third quarters of 2026. The limit on that reading is structural: each year is decided in a fourth quarter (topic 9) that management itself cannot see until the quarter closes.

Against the market. My view of guidance does not differ from the market's. The floors disappointed in February 2026, when they stood 43% below consensus profit; the market now understands them.

What would change my view. A range or a stated margin target in place of floors (Inderes expects one), or a capital markets day with dated mid-term targets.

Conclusion: Guidance is safely conservative and protects each report's downside, but a record of four missed growth guides and no raises means guidance will not supply a pattern of upgrades.

Score: 40, set by the Rater. Growth guidance was missed four years running, cut twice in 2025 and never raised, which weighs heavily; against that, cost, integration and conversion promises were met, margin guidance was met in 2023-24, today's floors are conservative (needing no organic growth) and revenue beat in three of four quarters from a low bar, so it sits close to the 45 guidance group, a little below because the miss record is longer than Instalco's.

5. Pricing power, leverage and feedback loops

Evidence. Four mechanisms turn revenue into profit at QT, and they differ in strength.

Price. Developer licences (about 60-65% of revenue) carry list-price increases of 5-10% a year, of which about 4.5% is realised after customers trim seats. The realised increase brings about EUR 7 million of new revenue a year at almost no cost, against wage inflation of about EUR 4 million, so price alone adds about 1.5 points of margin a year at flat volume. Royalty prices are fixed for the life of a design, so the royalty line has no price lever.

Operating leverage. About 85-90% of costs are fixed within a year, so a euro of licence revenue gained or lost moves EBITDA by about 90 cents. Across years the gearing is much lower, because management hires into growth: each extra euro of revenue added only 36-59 cents of EBITDA in 2022-2024. In 2025 the gearing ran in reverse, as revenue rose EUR 7 million and EBITDA fell EUR 19 million.

Financial leverage. Financial leverage is small and fading. Net debt of EUR 76.5 million at the end of September (1.3 times EBITDA) falls to about nil by the end of 2027, and lower interest adds about EUR 0.10 to EPS in 2027 and EUR 0.08 in 2028.

Feedback loops. The fastest feedback loop is an accounting one. Because revenue is recognised at signing, a customer who signs for three years instead of one turns 100 of annual contract value into about 255 of revenue today. In 2025 customers shortened their contracts and revenue fell. Those one-year contracts now renew every year, which could add 1-2 points to developer-licence growth in 2027 that the model does not include. A return to three-year terms would overshoot and leave a revenue gap two years later.

The slower loops help 2028-2030 more than 2027: design wins reach production as royalties after two to five years, IAR's subscription base builds, and accumulating cash lowers interest.

Inference. Revenue growth does produce outsized profit growth at QT: fully within a year and partly across years. Profit growth in 2027 owes almost nothing to this gearing, because it comes from self-help. From 2028 the model converts revenue growth of 7-8% into EBITDA growth of 10-14% and EPS growth of 11-20%.

So what. The gearing is asymmetric: a revenue shortfall hits profit in full within the year, while a revenue beat is shared with new hires. This asymmetry is why the range of outcomes is longer below the base case than above it (topic 9), and why price, which needs no volume, is the line to trust.

Counter-case. QT's annual price escalator can break. Earlier increases cost QT small customers, and customers answered the 2025 increases by buying the minimum number of seats.

Against the market. Consensus for 2028 implies that 67 cents of each extra euro of revenue reaches EBITDA, above anything in QT's record; the model uses 55 cents. I am therefore below the market on gearing after 2027.

What would change my view. Headcount held near 1,000 through a recovering 2027 would argue for higher gearing. Adoption of capacity-based pricing by existing customers would add a lever that no forecast includes.

Conclusion: QT has real pricing power and high in-year operating leverage, but management spends about 40% of the gearing across years, so outsized profit growth beyond 2027 depends on a hiring restraint that the record does not yet show.

Score: 74, set by the Rater. Two gears are proven: real pricing power (list rises of 5-10%, about 4.5% realised, held through the worst year in a decade, worth about 1.5 margin points a year at flat volume) and 85-90% of costs fixed within a year so a licence euro moves EBITDA about 90 cents, shown in reverse in 2025; financial leverage is small and fading, royalties have no price lever, and across years management has spent about 40% of the gearing on hiring (36-59 cents per euro in 2022-24), so the forecast 2028-30 ratio of EPS to revenue growth is only about twice, and it sits just below the 75 level.

The 2026 EBITDA margin is on FactSet's mixed basis, the 2024 EPS includes a one-off financial gain, and 2026-2027 free cash flow is slightly too high; the end notes give the details.

What the forecasts say.

  • One large step, then compounding. Model-basis EPS rises 51% in 2027, then 20%, 15% and 11%. On the consensus basis, EPS compounds at about 19% a year from 2027 to 2030, so double-digit EPS growth holds through the forecast horizon.
  • Against the past, the forecasts describe a restoration. Revenue grows at about a quarter of its 2019-2024 rate of about 29% a year. The margin returns to its 2023-2024 structure and regains the 2024 peak only around 2030. Consensus-basis EPS in 2027 returns to roughly the underlying 2024 level, and new ground is broken only from 2028.
  • Cash is the quiet feature. Free cash flow equals about 7% of today's market value in 2027 and about 9% in 2028. With nothing spent or returned, net cash reaches 28% of today's market value by the end of 2030.

How 2027 is built. EBITA rises by about EUR 26 million on the reported basis, and about 93% of the net rise comes from self-help that the business has already done (bridge below). By revenue line, the model's growth rates are in the small table that follows.

The assumptions I trust least. Testing tools grow 15% a year in the model, but they grew 6% in 2025 and the unit has no permanent head. Royalties grow 4% a year from 2028, against management's guidance of "flat to slightly lower".

So what. The forecasts support the case but do not, by themselves, make it a re-rating case. They describe a return to the economics of 2023-2024 on lower growth. Organic growth near 10%, management's own aim, would add about EUR 0.20-0.25 to 2028 EPS, and it is the difference between a restoration and a growth story.

Why I changed no input. My two main reservations about the model's inputs offset each other. The royalty line from 2028 is perhaps EUR 2 million a year too high, while the catch-up of one-year renewals could add EUR 2-3 million to 2027 developer licences. A third point is too small to matter: the bank loan amortises on a schedule to 2028, so 2028 interest could be EUR 0.5-1 million above the input, about EUR 0.02-0.03 a share. None of the three is large enough or well enough evidenced to move a forecast on which three independent builds agree.

Counter-case. DNB Carnegie models organic growth of 15% for 2027, on a recovery in customers' development programmes; a bear case of 2% organic growth is equally easy to write (topic 9).

Against the market. The model is in line with consensus on revenue and EPS and 3-4% below it on EBITDA, with a different revenue mix (topic 7).

What would change my view. Two reports will test the forecasts: the fourth-quarter cost base on 18 February and first-quarter growth in late April or May. The model's reference points are underlying fourth-quarter EBITDA of EUR 32 million, and first-quarter revenue growth of 8% with an EBITDA margin of 22%.

Conclusion: The forecasts offer double-digit EPS growth for four years from a mostly mechanical 2027 step, on growth well below the past and margins that restore the past without exceeding it.

Score: 90, set by the Rater. Growth of 15-30% gives A; placed at the floor because it is front-loaded (51% in 2027, then 20%, 15%, 11%), starts from a restructuring trough, and the margin only returns to its 2024 peak around 2030 on organic growth of about 7%, a quarter of the past rate.

7. Scope for upgrades to guidance, estimates and the narrative over 6-12 months

Evidence. Like for like, the model is on consensus. The one-page model summary shows the model's 2027 EPS 18% above consensus, but that gap is definitional (the model's EPS is before amortisation) and carries no view. The mix differs: the model is above consensus on licences and below it on royalties, where consensus has growth of 11% a year against management's guidance of "flat to slightly lower".

The brokers' 2026 figures are after restructuring costs, so the fourth quarter holds no hidden beat. Inderes shows a 2026 EBITA margin of 21.4% reported and 25.3% before restructuring, and the other brokers' EBITDA sits within about EUR 2 million of Inderes'. Consensus implies fourth-quarter revenue of about EUR 77 million and EBITA of about EUR 32 million, against the model's EUR 78 million and about EUR 30 million. I leave a 10-15% chance that the other brokers are on the more generous basis, in which case the quarter would beat consensus by about EUR 8 million.

The upgrade cycle of the last six months came from costs, and that source is used up: consensus 2027 EBITDA rose 28% on sales estimates only 5% higher.

Inference, event by event.

  • 18 February 2027 (fourth-quarter report). I expect an in-line quarter. Royalty estimates are likely to be trimmed by EUR 2-5 million (2-6% of EBITDA) once the 2026 outcome is known, while lower interest and a clean cost base push the other way. For the change in consensus 2027 EPS, I put 25% on a rise of more than 2%, 45% on little change and 30% on a cut of more than 2%.
  • Late April or May 2027 (first-quarter report). This is the first quarter with IAR in both periods, so reported growth will be close to organic growth. I put 45% on growth excluding IAR of 6-7% or better, which would start the first demand-led upgrades of the cycle, and 25% on growth of 4% or less, which would cut revenue estimates by 2-3% and EPS by 6-9%.
  • Guidance. Guidance will supply no upgrades (topic 4).
  • 2028 estimates. Consensus 2028 EBITDA is more likely to be trimmed by 3-6% during 2027 (on royalties and the 67-cent gearing), with EPS held because consensus financial costs are EUR 2.5-3.5 million too high.
  • The narrative. The market's narrative will change subject twice: from the size of the cost rebound (settled in February), to the organic growth rate (from April or May), to 2028 earnings power and the use of cash (from late 2027).

DNB Carnegie's figures in FactSet date from 6 August and carry 2027 revenue of EUR 287 million. When DNB Carnegie refreshes them, the consensus mean will fall and the median will not, so the median is the figure to quote.

So what. The scope for upgrades in the next six months is modest, and the February report may look soft: headline growth drops from +27% to about +1% for mechanical reasons, as IAR enters the comparison base. The scope in months 6 to 12 depends on one number, growth excluding IAR.

Counter-case. Several positive surprises sit in no forecast: the renewal catch-up; fourth-quarter costs EUR 2-3 million below the model; a stronger dollar (each 5% adds about 4.5% to EPS); a first buyback (the authorised 8% of shares would add about 8% to EPS); and visible licence conversions driven by the Cyber Resilience Act.

Against the market. The brokers describe the same recovery and reach the same numbers. I am more cautious than they are on royalties and on 2028 gearing, and more cautious than the Master Dashboard's momentum reading on how the February report will look.

What would change my view. A 2027 margin floor of 27% or more, organic ARR disclosed and growing above 10%, or first-quarter growth above 8%.

Conclusion: Upgrades over the next six months are unlikely to be material, because the cost-led upgrade cycle is complete and consensus equals my base case; the chance of demand-led upgrades in months 6 to 12 is a little under even.

Score: 45, set by the Rater. Guidance, which counts most, will be beaten and not raised (floors reiterated three times, 2027 floor likely set below consensus), consensus 2027 sits on the memo's base with royalties about EUR 5m too high and 2028 EBITDA more likely trimmed 3-6%, and the February report is as likely to cut as raise (25% up, 30% down); only months 6-12 carry a little-under-even chance of demand-led upgrades if growth ex-IAR reaches 6-7%, plus unmodelled dollar, renewal catch-up or buyback upside, so expected scope is about nil against 7.6% revenue growth, near the 47 group score.

8. Current momentum in guidance, estimates, narrative, price and peers

Evidence. The Master Dashboard's pinned ratings (snapshot of 11 November 2026) are A for technical momentum, B for sell-side earnings momentum (as at 10 November), B for thematic fit and momentum (as at 6 November) and A for valuation.

Price. The share price is up 29.5% over six months, down 11.9% over three and down 8.6% over twelve. It stands 14.8% above its 200-day average but below its 50-day average. The 200-day average rose in only 3 of the last 12 months, and QT's relative strength is at the 43rd percentile of the universe.

Estimates. Consensus 2027 EPS is up 8% over both one month and three months, and 46% over six; the mean target price is up 51% over six months. The share of buy ratings is 29%, down 14 points in a month.

Guidance. Guidance has no momentum: the floors have stood unchanged since February 2026.

Narrative. The narrative turned cooler in October, as investors looked through the headline revenue beat to the cleaner recurring measure. The third-quarter report beat on revenue and the shares fell, for reasons that fit that one theme: ARR rose only 1.8% in the quarter at comparable exchange rates, reported EBITA missed because of restructuring costs, guidance did not move, and Nordea stayed at Hold.

Peers. The sector is recovering stock by stock, and QT's price moves mostly on its own news: sector peers explain only about a fifth of its daily moves. Earnings momentum is A at Sectra, Sinch and Yubico, B at Planisware and Nemetschek, and F at TeamViewer, GB Group and Craneware. Innoscripta, the market's chosen "AI loser", is down 55% in a year. Eleven of QT's twenty sector peers sit at or below the 15th percentile of their own valuation history; the few in the upper half of their ranges, such as Planisware and Yubico, are the ones with visible growth.

Inference. Momentum is good on the six-month readings and weakening on the one-to-three-month readings. The sell-side momentum reading will fade by arithmetic alone: the six-month revision of +46% is measured from the trough of May 2026, so by February the window will show about +8% with no estimate changed, and by May about zero.

So what. QT's share price has followed its estimate revisions. Without new upgrades, momentum stops supporting the price around the February report, two to three months before the first evidence that could renew it.

Counter-case. The ratings may be right and my reading too cautious: a price well above a 200-day average that has started to rise, after a 16% pullback, is also how an early uptrend looks.

Against the market. The Master Dashboard reads momentum as strong. I read it as past its first peak, because the six-month revision window is about to roll past the May 2026 trough.

What would change my view. New upgrades of 2027 revenue (not costs) from any two brokers, or the price regaining its 50-day average on results.

Conclusion: Momentum is positive on the pinned ratings (technical A, sell-side B), but it is cost-led and ageing, and it will need demand-led revisions by spring 2027 to persist.

Score: 62, set by the Rater. One measure positive and one negative gives C; placed above mid-band because revisions are strong (3- and 6-month EPS revisions at the 96th-97th percentiles, +8% in three months is about the 83rd percentile against 7.6% revenue growth, price targets +51%), held down by a cooling narrative (shares fell 16% after a revenue beat, Buy share down 14 points to 29%), guidance unchanged and the price below its 50-day average with a barely rising 200-day.

9. Riskiness and simplicity of the forecasts

Evidence: what is simple. Three self-help items (the end of the restructuring charge, the savings and IAR) equal about 93% of the 2027 rise in EBITA. The balance sheet adds no risk: leverage stays below 1 times EBITDA even in the bear case. Costs can be tracked every quarter through headcount.

Evidence: what is fragile.

  • One quarter. About 42% of 2027 EBITDA is earned in the fourth quarter, on contracts signed in the last days of December.
  • Recognition. Because revenue is booked at signing, QT's one-year revenue forecast error is about 4-5%, against 1-2% for peers that recognise revenue over the contract term. With a fixed cost base, QT's range of EPS outcomes is three to four times as wide as theirs.
  • Open exposures. The dollar is unhedged, and royalties behave like lumpy deals.
  • Demand cannot be tracked. The developer-licence line, which carries 60% of revenue, mixes price, seats, contract length, testing and IAR, and QT does not disclose organic growth, IAR revenue or testing revenue.
  • The shares. Four brokers cover QT, about USD 4 million of its shares trade a day, and the stock is caught in two nervous themes (AI and cyclicals). A new AI coding release, a cluster of automotive warnings or a small-cap sell-off could take 20-30% off the price with no change in QT's numbers.

The range of 2027 outcomes. Base-case EBITDA is EUR 82 million, with an 80% range of about EUR 66-92 million; base-case EPS on the consensus basis is EUR 1.92, with a range of about EUR 1.40-2.20. In the bear case (20% probability), revenue is about EUR 236 million and EPS about EUR 1.27; the base case carries 60%; in the bull case (20%), revenue is about EUR 273 million and EPS EUR 2.26. I put the chance of reaching consensus EBITDA at 40-45%.

The five judgements, and what each is worth if wrong. The 2027 base case is revenue of EUR 262.3 million, EBITDA of EUR 82.4 million (31.4% margin) and EPS of EUR 1.92 on the consensus basis, with tax at 20% and 25.45 million shares. The table gives each judgement's arithmetic; the notes below it add the mechanisms.

  • Organic growth: one mechanism is enough. EUR 5-8 million of year-end contracts slipping into January (EUR 8 million did in 2024) would cost EUR 4.5-7 million of EBITDA, or 7-12% of EPS, and would return the following year. A 4-point shortfall would also cut free cash flow by about EUR 5 million, after EUR 2.8 million less working capital. This judgement also decides the multiple (topic 11).
  • Seats: the multiple is the larger exposure. The larger damage from fewer seats would be to the multiple, not to earnings. Testing growth of 15% would offset about EUR 6 million of lost seat revenue a year.
  • The first two judgements share a cause. Organic growth and royalties both depend on device makers' budgets, and both went wrong together in 2025. Together with a weaker dollar, they make up the bear case.

Suddenness and precedents. Bad news has come suddenly at QT: profit warnings came in October 2025 and in the first days of January 2024 and January 2025. Floor guidance removes the trigger for a formal profit warning but leaves the risk of a shortfall against consensus. The sector's precedents add one lesson to those in topics 2 and 8: margin restorations that came from costs, on single-digit growth, were not re-rated (Open Text, Temenos, Sprout Social, Trend Micro). QT's own multiple fell from 57 times at the end of 2021 to 17 times nine months later, and from 25 to 11 times between early 2025 and early 2026.

How far the shares could fall. A trough multiple of 11-12 times on bear-case earnings two years ahead gives about EUR 18-22 a share, around the 52-week low of EUR 18.04. At EUR 20 the enterprise value would be about 7 times 2027 EBITDA, against the 15-20 times at which private-equity buyers underwrite software exits, so a private-equity bid becomes plausible near that price. A possible bid is a cushion and not a guarantee, because any bid would need the support of the largest shareholder.

So what. The risk in QT is about the level and timing of one year's profit, not about direction or solvency. The risk resolves late, in the February report after each December, and it cannot be tracked in between.

Counter-case. The case may be safer than this section suggests. About four fifths of the 2027 earnings step needs nothing the business has not already done, and even with no organic growth at all, 2027 EBITDA would be about EUR 67 million, above 2026.

Against the market. The separate risk research put the probability that the case fails at 35-40%. I put the chance that 2027 EBITDA lands more than 15% below consensus at about 20%, because the earnings step rests on costs and price. The shares' reaction to any miss would, however, be larger than the miss itself.

What would change my view. Disclosure of organic ARR and of IAR revenue would cut the tracking risk more than any result, and a hedging policy would remove one of the five judgements.

Conclusion: The case is simple to state and predictable in costs, price and direction, but the level of any one year's profit is risky because of December concentration, upfront recognition, royalties and an unhedged dollar, and the bear case takes about a third off the share price.

Score: 40, set by the Rater. The 2027 EPS cone is about -27%/+15% (EUR 1.40-2.20 around 1.92) and skewed down, with 42% of EBITDA earned in one December quarter, revenue booked at signing on a fixed cost base, an unhedged dollar, lumpy royalties, undisclosed organic growth and a history of sudden warnings, on four brokers and AI/cyclical sentiment that could take 20-30% off the price; low leverage, self-help that is 93% of the step and a low multiple bound it, coherent with the 38 and 60 risk groups.

10. Where the stock is in its lifecycle

Evidence. The bottom is behind QT. Estimates troughed in May 2026 (consensus 2027 EPS was EUR 1.36 then and is EUR 1.99 now), and the share price troughed in the spring at about EUR 18. Since the bottom, the stock has completed only the first half of a turn. Estimates have risen on costs, while 2027 revenue estimates remain 9% below their level of a year ago. The multiple fell while estimates rose, one broker sits at Hold, the share of buy ratings has dropped, and a revenue beat was sold.

Inference. The Master Dashboard's rule places the stock in the Broadening phase. I place it one phase earlier, in Turning up. A thesis broadens when new kinds of evidence and new buyers arrive: revenue-led revisions, a rising multiple and widening broker coverage. None of the three has appeared yet.

So what. The phase matters for two reasons. It defines the next evidence the stock needs, which is demand, since the cost story is known. And it sets the fair multiple under the guideline, which gives a turning-up stock a lower place in its historical range than a broadening one (topic 11).

The paths from here, by mid-2027. I see three paths (figure below). Broadening is the most likely, at about 45%. Staying in Turning up, or stalling, is about 35%. Falling back, which is the bear case of topic 9, is about 20%.

Counter-case. The Master Dashboard may simply be early and right. The price has held far above its low through a 16% pullback, and the first-quarter mechanics (a margin up about 10 points on the year, and growth free of the IAR distortion) could move the stock into Broadening on a single report.

Against the market. The price action of October says that investors also see an incomplete turn; on the phase, I am with the market and against the Master Dashboard's label.

What would change my view. Any broker raising 2027 revenue by 3% or more on demand, or the multiple rising through a quarter in which estimates also rise.

Conclusion: The stock is turning up and past its bottom, with about an even chance of broadening by mid-2027 if organic growth shows.

Score: 63, set by the Rater. The memo's Turning up is right over the computed Broadening: estimates and price bottomed in May and the cost-led upgrade cycle is done, but revenue estimates are still 9% below a year ago, the multiple fell as estimates rose and a beat was sold, with momentum due to fade before the first clean organic print; an early-to-mid turn with about an even chance of broadening by mid-2027.

11. The fair multiple

The guideline. The Master Dashboard gives a fair multiple of 43.04 times two-year-forward earnings: the 80th percentile of the stock's own ten-year history, which is the place the guideline assigns to a stock in the Broadening phase.

My viewThe guideline's rule misfires for QT, and 43 times is far above what the evidence supports. Four reasons follow.
  1. The ten-year history describes a different company. The ten-year range (median 29 times, 90th percentile 53 times) was earned at growth of 20-50% a year, against a forecast of 7-8%. At the guideline's value of about EUR 140 a share, QT would be valued at about 12.5 times 2028 revenue and 40 times 2028 EBITA; Schneider is paying 8 times revenue and 21 times EBITA for PTC, including a control premium.
  2. The sector does not pay 43 times. The sector median is about 15 times. The comparators nearest to QT in growth and margin run from 15 times (Sage) and 17 times (Dassault Systèmes) to 20 times (Nemetschek) and 23 times (Planisware, which grows 13-14% with a 37% margin).
  3. The phase is one step earlier (topic 10), which on the guideline's own logic points to a lower place in the range.
  4. The EPS bases do not match. The percentile bands were measured on consensus EPS, after amortisation, but the model applies them to EPS before amortisation, which is 11-20% higher. That mismatch alone inflates the value. The mismatch also explains why the model's re-rating (+299%, from 10.8 times) is larger than the Master Dashboard's own (+193%, from 14.7 times). The dashboard's 14.7 times appears to be the September month-end reading, at a price of EUR 33.8; at today's price the same series would show about 13 times, in line with FactSet's 13.4 times.

What I can defend. On the consensus basis, two years forward:

  • 16 to 20 times for the next 18 months. Sixteen times is the stock's own median of the last two years and the 10th percentile of its ten-year range; it fits a case that stays cost-led but proves its margin. Twenty times needs organic growth visibly in the high single digits.
  • 22 to 24 times only with growth near 10% and a recovered sector; 24 times is QT's five-year median and about Planisware's rating.
  • 11 to 13 times if growth disappoints or AI fears return; the five-year low is 11.25 times.

The guideline's rule can be kept with a repaired reference period. Applying the same 80th percentile to the last 24 months of the series (October 2024 to September 2026) instead of the last ten years gives about 22 times (my calculation from the monthly figures), at the bottom of the 22-24 times band above.

Cross-checks. The brokers' targets of EUR 37-41 equal about 13 times 2027 EBITA, or 19-21 times 2027 EPS on the consensus basis. Inderes' scenarios run from EUR 30 (growth of 5%, margin of 25%) to EUR 95 (growth of 14%, margin of 38%). DNB Carnegie's cash-flow value is EUR 76 and its peer-multiple value EUR 25; the gap between the two shows how much of any higher value rests on growth returning.

So what. The organic growth rate will decide the multiple, so the report dates in topic 7 are also the dates on which the fair multiple is tested.

Counter-case. Software multiples have moved 30% or more within a year, and QT's franchise quality could justify a premium to the sector sooner than I allow. The strongest evidence against any re-rating is in topic 9: cost-led restorations on single-digit growth have not been re-rated.

Against the market. The market pays about 13 times. I think 16 to 20 times is fair if 2027 is delivered, so I am above the market and far below the guideline.

What would change my view. Organic growth of 10% or more for several quarters, or a change in the pricing unit away from seats, would move me toward the mid-20s. Nothing in view moves me toward 43 times.

Conclusion: The guideline's 43 times is not a fair multiple for a business forecast to grow 7-8%; I can defend 16 to 20 times on the consensus basis, and up to 24 times if growth near 10% returns.

Score: 90, set by the Rater. Cheap on both gives A, placed at the floor because much of the cheapness is deserved: the ten-year range was earned at 20-50% growth against 7-8% now and the phase is turning up, not broadening; yet the memo's defensible 16-20x still sits well above today's 13x, so the business warrants more than the market pays.

12. Total shareholder return

The model's return, at the guideline multiple.

What drives the modelled return.

  • The multiple. The model moves the two-year-forward multiple from 10.8 times today to 43.04 times by March 2028 and holds it there. That one assumption quadruples the price; without it, the model's return to March 2028 is +15%.
  • Earnings. Two-year-forward EPS on the model basis rises about 15% by March 2028 and 30% by September 2029, about 10% a year. The earnings leg looks small beside the 51% jump in 2027 EPS because a two-year-forward measure already contains the 2027 recovery. The market is already pricing 2028 earnings, so the mechanical rebound is in the starting price; what the earnings leg adds is the compounding after the rebound: organic growth of about 7%, 55 cents of EBITDA on each extra euro of revenue, and falling interest.
  • Dividends and other cash returns. None. The company has never paid a dividend, and the model assumes no buyback. Cash builds instead, to about EUR 2.3 a share at the end of 2028 and EUR 5.3 at the end of 2029, which a price-to-earnings value does not count.

My reading: the same earnings at multiples the evidence supports. I convert the model's horizon EPS to the consensus basis (about EUR 2.91 at March 2028 and EUR 3.37 at September 2029, after deducting my estimate of amortisation) and apply the range from topic 11. On the same basis, today's multiple is 12.5 times.

Inference. Three statements hold whatever multiple is right.

  1. With no re-rating, the return comes from earnings alone: about 10% a year on the model basis and 12-14% on the consensus basis, where a fixed amortisation charge shrinks against growing profit.
  2. Each turn of the multiple is worth about EUR 2.9 a share, or 10% of today's price, so the multiple outweighs any plausible error in the earnings forecast.
  3. The multiple will follow the organic growth rate, which makes judgement 1 of topic 9 the driver of both the earnings and the multiple.
Probability-weighted returnWeighting the paths of topic 10 (45% re-rating to 16-20 times, 35% no re-rating, 20% bear case at about EUR 20) gives a return of roughly +30% to March 2028. The weighting is my rough estimate; the model holds no scenarios.

So what. The attraction of QT is the shape of the payoff, and the guideline's headline return hides that shape. The bear case costs about a third. The no-re-rating case earns a low-teens annual return from earnings that are mostly secured. A return to a sector-level or slightly better multiple, which needs growth QT has delivered in most of its years, adds 50-90%.

Counter-case. The no-re-rating outcome may persist for longer than 18 months, as it did for Open Text and Temenos. And QT may spend its cash on a large acquisition at five times revenue, as it did with IAR, instead of returning the cash to shareholders.

Against the market. The brokers' mean target of about EUR 38, a 12-month figure, lies between my no-re-rating value (EUR 36) and my 16-times value (EUR 47). I am above the brokers if growth shows, and level with them if it does not.

What would change my view. A buyback would lift the lower values by up to 8% and show that cash can come back to shareholders. An acquisition before organic growth is proven would lower the multiple I can defend.

Conclusion: The modelled +359% is almost entirely a re-rating I cannot support; at 16 to 20 times the evidence supports a return of roughly 50-90% by March 2028, driven by earnings growth of a little over 10% a year and a partial recovery of the multiple, with nothing from dividends.

Score: 80, set by the Rater. About +30% sits in the B band (about 85 on the scale); moved down for a fat lower tail (a third lost in the bear case) and because the gain above +19% runs through a re-rating, with nothing from dividends; the modelled +359% at the guideline multiple is set aside, as the memo argues.

13. Summary conclusion

QT Group is a strong franchise coming out of a self-inflicted and cyclical trough. The 2027 earnings recovery is the most predictable forecast this company has offered in years, because it rests on costs already cut, prices already raised, a restructuring charge that ends and a subscription base that builds through revenue recognition. The recovery is in consensus and, on a two-year view, in the share price, so it will surprise no one.

What is not in the price is any credit for growth. The shares sit at about 13 times, a little below a depressed sector, after a year in which the market learned to distrust this company's revenue. The next 18 months therefore turn on one question that the company does not yet let anyone measure directly: whether the business excluding IAR grows nearer 4% or 7%. At 7%, estimates start to rise for the right reason, the phase moves from turning up to broadening, and a multiple of 16 to 20 times becomes reasonable. At 4%, the investor still owns a 30%-margin business compounding earnings at close to 10% a year, with net cash arriving in 2028, at a multiple near the bottom of its history.

Richard's test: a two-part answerThe probability of upgrades is not skewed to the positive today: guidance will not be raised, consensus equals my base case, and the February report is more likely to look soft than strong. The share value is skewed to the positive, because a low multiple, falling debt and a secured cost base bound the downside, while the upside needs only ordinary growth.

Three dates matter most: 18 February 2027 (the cost base, the 2027 floors and royalties), late April or May 2027 (the first clean growth figure) and February 2028 (the fourth quarter that decides 2027). The return shown at the guideline multiple should be set aside; the case stands without it.

Thesis's Change Forces' Strength: 70, set by the Rater. A strong, largely executed internal reset (topic 2, 68) reaches profits surely, giving A-grade forecast EPS growth of about 23% a year (topic 6), but it is a restoration to 2024 economics led by costs and the external forces are only mildly positive (topic 1, 55), so the net change is clearly positive yet short of the funded external-plus-internal force of the high 70s.

Foundations' Robustness: 70, set by the Rater. A dominant, high-switching-cost, capital-light franchise with pricing power proven under stress (topic 3, 72) is robust in structure, but four years of missed growth guides (topic 4, 40), upfront recognition that makes results lumpy, a thin bench and a low-return acquisition keep it below the 75 band where delivery or stability would match the franchise.

Setup's Fit/Crispness: 70, set by the Rater. The case fits 'cause for concern (CfC) in quality cyclical at trough-on-trough, leading to reversion to normal' in substance: a quality franchise at its 2025-26 trough with the cost cause for concern cleared and margins reverting; current problems (US sales, a headless testing unit, organic growth not yet shown) and an AI seat question that a cycle does not clear blur it below the 75 level.

Case Riskiness: 40, set by the Rater. Following topic 9 (40): simple to state with low leverage, conservative floors and a multiple near the bottom of its range, but next year's profit turns on one December quarter booked at signing, open dollar and royalty exposures and thin, theme-driven trading, so a miss shows suddenly and the bear case costs about a third.

End notes

Forecasts and research. The forecasts are those of the Financial Analyst's model (update 2); I have changed no input (topic 6 gives the reasons). The latest Earnings Review in the research covers the third quarter of 2026 (interim report of 29 October 2026), so it is current.

Bases. EPS on the model basis is before the amortisation of acquired intangibles; on the consensus basis it is after that amortisation. In 2027 the two differ by about EUR 0.39 a share. Each chart states its basis. The 2027 EBITA bridge uses the memo's rounded steps, so its ends are approximate.

The forecast table in topic 6. The 2026 EBITDA margin is on FactSet's mixed basis (after the second quarter's restructuring cost, before the third quarter's); fully underlying, it is 27.0%. The 2024 EPS of EUR 2.26 included a one-off financial gain; underlying, it was about EUR 2.0. Free cash flow in 2026-2027 is a few million euros too high, because the model does not yet deduct restructuring cash.

Sources of the visuals. Default charts and tables come from the Financial Analyst's model (update 2), FactSet and the Master Dashboard, as noted under each. Charts drawn for this page (the EBITA bridge, the quarterly shape, the range of outcomes, the five judgements, the map of multiples, the value ladder, the payoff by path and the cash build) take their figures from the memo text and the recent-periods table.

Quarterly estimates. The fourth quarter of 2026 and the first quarter of 2027 in the quarterly chart are the model's reference figures quoted in topic 6, not separate forecasts; the fourth-quarter 2026 EBITDA margin is underlying, while the actual quarters are reported.
